clue.text: Succession, say, for Demeter

indicators.note: say tells the solver to go by how a word is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: a succession of things is a series

explanation.surface: A question of who follows whom in the line of the harvest goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: SERIES (succession), spoken, gives the name of Demeter's Roman counterpart.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess of grain was identified with the Greek Demeter.

clue.text: Bentham's world hardly visible from that of Pangloss

definitions.text: Bentham's world hardly visible from that of Pangloss

parts.words: Bentham's world hardly visible from that of Pangloss
parts.note: Bentham coined a word for the worst imaginable state, far from Pangloss's best world

explanation.surface: Bentham's view of the world seen from Voltaire's optimist.
explanation.walkthrough: Pangloss in Candide holds this is the best of all possible worlds; Bentham named the opposite, the worst-governed place.
explanation.definitionFit: Bentham coined the term for an imagined worst society, the opposite of utopia.

clue.text: "There was a lovely yellow — of sunflowers in the garden" (D. H. Lawrence, Sons and Lovers)

definitions.text: "There was a lovely yellow — of sunflowers in the garden" (D. H. Lawrence, Sons and Lovers)

parts.words: "There was a lovely yellow — of sunflowers in the garden" (D. H. Lawrence, Sons and Lovers)
parts.note: the missing word in Lawrence's line is a tangle of sunflowers

explanation.surface: A gap in a line from Sons and Lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a tangle, here a tangled mass of sunflowers in Lawrence's sentence.

clue.text: His best work was over the weekend

definitions.text: His best work was over the weekend

parts.words: His best work was over the weekend
parts.note: the novelist's best-known book is titled Saturday Night and Sunday Morning

explanation.surface: Someone produced his best output on a Saturday and Sunday.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Sillitoe wrote Saturday Night and Sunday Morning, a title spanning the weekend.

clue.text: Rossetti's little flame

parts.note: a Rossetti poem bears an Italian woman's name meaning a small flame

explanation.surface: A Pre-Raphaelite poet's small fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante Gabriel Rossetti wrote a sonnet titled with this Italian name, which literally means a small blaze.

clue.text: Liberated Dreiser's book

definitions.meaning: Theodore Dreiser's story collection ... and Other Stories

explanation.surface: Dreiser's book was released.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberated means at liberty; Dreiser published a collection titled with this word.

clue.text: O Absalom -he encouraged your conspiracy

parts.note: the counsellor who backed Absalom's revolt against David in the Bible

explanation.surface: A lament addressed to Absalom about his co-plotter.
explanation.definitionFit: In 2 Samuel, David's counsellor joined Absalom's rebellion; Dryden made him Shaftesbury in Absalom and Achitophel.

clue.text: False character of D'Urfey

parts.note: Thomas D'Urfey's comedy Madam Fickle names a fickle lady

explanation.surface: An untrue figure in a Restoration playwright's work.
explanation.walkthrough: D'Urfey's play is Madam Fickle; 'False' stands for fickle, the character being the title's form of address.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character's form of address in D'Urfey's Madam Fickle is the French word for a married lady.

clue.text: They had an invitation to the ballet

definitions.text: They had an invitation to the ballet

parts.words: They had an invitation to the ballet
parts.note: Jerome Robbins made a ballet about people invited to a party

explanation.surface: People invited to an evening at the ballet.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome Robbins's 1949 ballet is named for those who are invited.

clue.text: Version of 10 prepared to defend itself

indicators.note: a version is a reworking, so the letters of the other answer are rearranged

parts.note: 10 refers to the answer to clue 10, a night-time vision

explanation.surface: A form of another answer that is ready for battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Being equipped with weapons means being ready to fight back.

clue.text: Horseman I identified with Medici court composer

parts.note: a cavalier is a mounted soldier or rider
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rider claims to be the musician at the Florentine court.
explanation.definitionFit: Emilio de' Cavalieri was a composer employed at the Medici court in Florence around 1600.

clue.text: Church vision

parts.note: a vision seen in sleep, perhaps of the kind religious writers describe

explanation.surface: A religious revelation in a cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: A vision seen while sleeping is the night-time imagining the clue describes.

clue.text: Vital listening, including sacred music composer

indicators.note: including says the answer is held within the words that come before it

explanation.surface: Careful listening is essential to appreciate a church composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'including' points to the run of letters spanning the end of 'Vital' and the start of 'listening'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Tallis was a Tudor composer of English church music.

clue.text: Pile made from ghostwritten ghost story by H. P. Lovecraft

definitions.meaning: a pile is a heap or raised bank of earth

definitions.text: ghostwritten ghost story by H. P. Lovecraft
definitions.meaning: a weird tale Lovecraft wrote under Zealia Bishop's name

explanation.surface: A heap emerges from a horror tale Lovecraft wrote for someone else.
explanation.definitionFit: A heap is a raised pile of earth; Lovecraft ghostwrote a novella of this title for Zealia Bishop.

clue.text: Villainous Greek pores hopelessly over meagre ration

indicators.note: over means the jumbled letters spread across and around the next piece
hopelessly suggests the word pores is thrown into disorder

parts.note: a crust of bread is a meagre ration

explanation.surface: A wicked Greek studies a tiny portion in despair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Villainous Greek' is the mythical bandit who made travellers fit his bed by stretching or lopping them; 'hopelessly' scrambles the pores and 'over' wraps the result round the crust.
explanation.definitionFit: Procrustes was the Greek bandit who stretched or cut his guests to fit his bed.

clue.text: Ancient UK resident put circle on diagram as a symbol

parts.note: the Picts were ancient inhabitants of northern Britain
a circle is shaped like the letter O
a graph is a kind of diagram

explanation.surface: An early Briton draws a ring on a chart to stand for something.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture standing for a word or idea is a pictorial symbol.

clue.text: Like Hay's days in Spain

parts.note: John Hay wrote a travel book called ... Days

explanation.surface: Resembling an American writer's time spent in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: John Hay's travel book about Spain is Castilian Days, so the adjective describes it.

clue.text: Man, perhaps, in Disraeli's Letters

indicators.note: in says the answer sits within the words that follow it

explanation.surface: A man may be mentioned in the correspondence of the Victorian prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea, not a person; the letters run across the end of 'Disraeli's' and the start of 'Letters'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is an example of an island.

clue.text: Oz book may be in another location

definitions.meaning: an Australian book of this title

explanation.surface: An Australian book may be found somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oz' is slang for Australia, not the Wizard's land.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means somewhere else, and is also the title of an Australian book.

clue.text: Mitford's stately home

parts.note: Mary Russell Mitford's novel is named for a grand country house

explanation.surface: A great house belonging to one of the Mitfords.
explanation.walkthrough: This is Mary Russell Mitford, the Regency author of Our Village, not one of the twentieth-century Mitford sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Russell Mitford's 1854 novel takes its name from the country estate at its centre.

clue.text: Afterthought, in Irish poet, describes end of church

indicators.note: in says the first piece sits inside the second

parts.note: AE was the pen name of the Irish poet George Russell
PS, postscript, is an afterthought to a letter

explanation.surface: An Irish writer's postscript depicts the far end of a church.
explanation.definitionFit: The rounded east end of a church is the vaulted recess beyond the altar.

clue.text: Snowdrift separated them from literary intellectuals

definitions.text: Snowdrift separated them from literary intellectuals

parts.words: Snowdrift separated them from literary intellectuals
parts.note: C. P. Snow's argument in The Two Cultures split the lab from the arts

explanation.surface: Drifting snow cut one group off from the bookish crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snowdrift' is the drift of C. P. Snow's lecture The Two Cultures, which divided researchers in the natural sciences from literary people.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow's Two Cultures lecture contrasted researchers in physics and chemistry with literary intellectuals.

clue.text: The mind of Michael Roberts

parts.note: Michael Roberts wrote The ... Mind

explanation.surface: What went on in a poet-critic's head.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Roberts's 1937 study is The Modern Mind; the word means up to date.

clue.text: Novel afterthought

parts.note: the closing section added after a novel's main story

explanation.surface: A fresh idea that came late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like 'new' but means a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A concluding section after a book's main narrative is its afterword.

clue.text: Also French with this Latin system of morals

parts.note: et is French for and, also
hic is Latin for this

explanation.surface: A French and Latin mix forms a code of conduct.
explanation.definitionFit: A set of moral principles is a moral code.

clue.text: American novelist in with a shout

explanation.surface: An American writer is in contention.
explanation.definitionFit: Saul Bellow was an American novelist; to roar is to shout loudly.

clue.text: He took all in Greeneland

parts.note: Graham Greene wrote a novella in which this person Takes All

explanation.surface: A man swept the board in Greene's fictional world.
explanation.walkthrough: Graham Greene's novella is The Loser Takes All; 'Greeneland' is critics' name for Greene's fictional world.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's title names the one who fails as taking everything, an ironic reversal.

parts.note: taken as written
ein is German for one

explanation.surface: A poet whose collection features a German.
explanation.definitionFit: Heinrich Heine was a German poet.

clue.text: Courteously greeted by Sagan

explanation.surface: Someone politely welcomed by a French novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Françoise Sagan's novel is Bonjour Tristesse: sadness is greeted with 'good day'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for sadness follows 'Bonjour' in the title of Sagan's first novel.
